---
title: "Prompt Injection"
description: "An attack in which untrusted content attempts to override an AI system's intended instructions or influence its actions."
term: "Prompt Injection"
letter: "P"
category: "AI Safety"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Prompt injection is a way of tricking an AI application by putting
instruction-like text in a place the model is meant to treat as data. For
example, a document being summarized could contain a message telling the
assistant to ignore its task and reveal private information.

## Technical explanation

An injection exploits the fact that language models process instructions and
ordinary text in a shared context. It may be direct (entered by a user) or
indirect (embedded in retrieved pages, files, emails, or tool output). The
model may follow the attacker-supplied text if the application has not
reliably separated trusted instructions, untrusted content, and authorized
actions.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Applications that retrieve external content or call tools can turn a
misleading model response into data exposure or unauthorized action.
Prompt-injection resistance therefore needs to be considered in system
architecture, permissions, and testing, not only in the wording of a prompt.

## How it works

The attacker places a conflicting directive in content the model will read.
If the model treats that text as authoritative, it may change its response or
attempt a tool call. Mitigations include restricting tool permissions,
validating and constraining actions outside the model, isolating sensitive
data, and testing indirect-injection paths; no prompt wording alone
guarantees prevention.

## Practical example

A retrieval-augmented assistant is asked to summarize a web page. The page
contains text instructing the assistant to email its hidden system prompt.
Treat the page as untrusted input, prevent the model from accessing secrets,
and require an independent authorization check before any external action.

## Common misconceptions

- Delimiters and phrases such as “ignore instructions in the document” may
  help communicate intent but are not a security boundary.
- A model's refusal to follow one test injection does not prove that the
  whole application is safe.
